title: Economic Outlook and the Labor Market
summary: Vice Chair Philip N. Jefferson delivered a speech on April 7, 2026 presenting his economic outlook, noting that while the economy is growing at pace with potential (2% GDP), inflation remains above the 2% target with PCE at 2.8% and core PCE at 3.0% as of February. The labor market is described as roughly in balance, with the unemployment rate at 4.3% in March 2026, though job growth has slowed to an average of 70,000 per month in Q1.
key_points: PCE inflation at 2.8% and core PCE at 3.0% for 12 months ending February 2026, with little progress in lowering core inflation over the past year
Unemployment rate rose from 4.0% in January 2025 to 4.5% in November 2025, then edged lower to 4.3% in March 2026
March 2026 payrolls added 178,000 jobs; Q1 2026 average pace of ~70,000 jobs per month, described as somewhat subdued but within breakeven range
Tariffs cited as the main reason progress on disinflation has stalled over the past year
Energy prices noted as adding upward pressure to headline inflation in the near term; ongoing trade policy uncertainty and geopolitical tensions pose upside risks to inflation forecast
Vice Chair sees risks to both sides of the dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices
why_it_matters: This speech from the Federal Reserve Vice Chair provides the market with current FOMC thinking on the economic outlook. With PCE inflation remaining at 2.8-3.0% and the Fed still committed to the 2% target, traders will assess the likelihood and timing of any rate adjustments. The labor market's gradual cooling while staying near the natural rate of unemployment suggests the Fed has room to remain patient. The explicit acknowledgment that tariffs have stalled disinflation and that energy prices will add near-term pressure to headline inflation informs expectations about the policy path.
macro_context: The speech presents a balanced macroeconomic outlook with growth continuing near potential (2% GDP) supported by consumer spending, business investment, and AI-related capital spending. Inflation remains elevated due to tariffs and energy prices, while the labor market has cooled gradually without significant layoffs. The Fed Vice Chair explicitly notes that progress on disinflation has stalled and that both energy prices and trade policy uncertainty pose upside risks to inflation. The dual-mandate risks described suggest the Fed is in a wait-and-see mode.
important_numbers: 3.0% core PCE inflation (12 months ending February 2026)
